prerequisites: No prior requirements are needed to take the Materials Science course, only basic principles of physics, chemistry, mechanics, and thermodynamics.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge of basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Knowledge of atomic structures and their defects and the ability to control material properties by modifying atomic structures with defects.
Knowledge of the magnitudes that define the different properties characterizing the behavior of industrial materials.
Knowledge of phase diagrams enabling them to handle binary equilibrium diagrams and the fundamentals of ternary diagrams with ease.
Knowledge of the fundamentals of materials science, technology, and chemistry. Understand the relationship between microstructure, synthesis or processing, and the properties of metallic materials.
Ability to design heat treatments to modify the microstructure and properties of steels, cast irons, and non-ferrous alloys.
Ability to use diverse materials and combine them appropriately to design composite materials with controlled properties.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Basic knowledge of concepts related to product verification and inspection and ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Identify the structures of fundamental crystalline solids and assess the importance of different structural defects.
Interpret the different properties of materials and also be able to determine them experimentally using appropriate testing techniques.
Interpret equilibrium diagrams and use them in material development.

Fluently handle the Fe-C diagram, transformation curves, evaluate the influence of alloying elements in these products, the practical use of Jominy hardenability curves for steels, and the effects of heat treatments.
Discern the main characteristics of non-ferrous alloys of industrial interest that justify their application, assess the importance of alloying elements, and the effects of heat treatments.
Differentiate the different families of plastic, ceramic, and composite materials, their main characteristics, their advantages and limitations for industrial use.
Ability to define the fundamental characteristics that describe crystalline structures.
Ability to use diffusion laws for various calculations.
Ability to determine the conventional mechanical properties of industrial materials based on the performance of corresponding experimental tests.
Ability to determine electrical, magnetic, thermal, and optical properties from experimental methods.
Ability to interpret binary equilibrium diagrams and to plot points and determine phases present in ternary diagrams.
Ability to interpret the Fe-C diagram and the transformation curves of steels and cast irons to modify their microstructure and properties through mechanical and thermal treatments.
Ability to prepare metallographic specimens, perform heat treatments, and interpret the microstructures of iron-based materials.
Ability to interpret the base equilibrium diagrams of the most important non-ferrous metallic alloys and use them to define their characteristic heat treatments.
Ability to manage and interpret equilibrium diagrams in ceramic systems and to control their properties based on their manufacturing processes.
Ability to interpret the mechanical properties of plastics based on their structural characteristics and manufacturing processes.
Ability to calculate the properties of composite materials from those of the simple materials that constitute them.
Foster in the student an interest in the acquisition of scientific knowledge.
Lay the groundwork for the student to be able to apply the acquired knowledge in engineering.
Formation of an open, critical, and entrepreneurial spirit.

syllabus_topics: Crystallography. Metallographic preparation and grain size determination.
Microstructures of steels and cast irons.
assessment_rules: For continuous evaluation, a minimum grade of 4 (out of 10) is required in the final exam, with a minimum of 30% of the value of each of its three parts (laboratory practices, theory, and exercises), and the overall grade must be 5 or higher. For non-continuous evaluation, a final exam covering all course content is given, divided into three parts: laboratory practices (1 point), theory and exercises (9 points). To pass this exam, a grade of 5 or higher is required, with a minimum of 30% of the value of each of the three parts. Students who did not pass by continuous evaluation may take extraordinary exams following the criteria of non-continuous evaluation.
